d14:b317.text: Make too many OAuth access token requests in a short period of time. No more than 2,000 OAuth access token requests per hour are allowed for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps.
d14:b317.heading: Rate limits for the REST API > About secondary rate limits
section_context: Rate limits for the REST API

d14:b291.text: All of these requests count towards your personal rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour. Requests made on your behalf by a GitHub App that is owned by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization have a higher rate limit of 15,000 requests per hour. Similarly, requests made on your behalf by a OAuth app that is owned or approved by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization have a higher rate limit of 15,000 requests per hour if you are a member of the GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization. However, requests made by a higher-limit app reduce the remaining budget available for lower-limit authentication methods. For example, if an app with a 15,000 request limit makes 10,000 requests on your behalf, you will have exhausted the 5,000 request budget for your personal access tokens, even though the app has 5,000 requests remaining.
d14:b291.heading: Rate limits for the REST API > About primary rate limits > Primary rate limit for authenticated users
section_context: Rate limits for the REST API
Primary rate limit for authenticated users

d14:b293.text: API requests are required when you upload or download Git LFS content. These count towards a separate rate limiting bucket with a limit of 300 requests per minute for unauthenticated requests and 3,000 requests per minute for authenticated requests.
d14:b293.heading: Rate limits for the REST API > About primary rate limits > Primary rate limit for Git LFS access
section_context: Rate limits for the REST API
Primary rate limit for Git LFS access

d14:b294.text: Git LFS uses a batch API which processes 100 Git LFS objects per API request by default. That means unauthenticated users can download 30,000 Git LFS objects per minute and authenticated users can upload/download 300,000 Git LFS objects per minute.
d14:b294.heading: Rate limits for the REST API > About primary rate limits > Primary rate limit for Git LFS access
section_context: Rate limits for the REST API
Primary rate limit for Git LFS access

d14:b305.text: Never include your app's client secret in client-side code or in code that runs on a user device. The client secret can be used to generate OAuth access tokens for users who have authorized your app, so you should always keep the client secret secure.
d14:b305.heading: Rate limits for the REST API > About primary rate limits > Primary rate limit for OAuth apps
section_context: Rate limits for the REST API
Primary rate limit for OAuth apps

d14:b312.text: Make too many concurrent requests. No more than 100 concurrent requests are allowed. This limit is shared across the REST API and GraphQL API.
d14:b312.heading: Rate limits for the REST API > About secondary rate limits
section_context: Rate limits for the REST API

d14:b313.text: Make too many requests to a single endpoint per minute. No more than 900 points per minute are allowed for REST API endpoints, and no more than 2,000 points per minute are allowed for the GraphQL API endpoint. For more information about points, see Calculating points for the secondary rate limit .
d14:b313.heading: Rate limits for the REST API > About secondary rate limits
section_context: Rate limits for the REST API

d14:b316.text: Create too much content on GitHub in a short amount of time. In general, no more than 80 content-generating requests per minute and no more than 500 content-generating requests per hour are allowed. Some endpoints have lower content creation limits. Content creation limits include actions taken on the GitHub web interface as well as via the REST API and GraphQL API.
d14:b316.heading: Rate limits for the REST API > About secondary rate limits
section_context: Rate limits for the REST API

d14:b335.text: If you want a higher primary rate limit, consider making authenticated requests instead of unauthenticated requests. Authenticated requests have a significantly higher rate limit than unauthenticated requests.
d14:b335.heading: Rate limits for the REST API > Getting a higher rate limit
section_context: Rate limits for the REST API

d14:b283.text: GitHub limits the number of REST API requests that you can make within a specific amount of time. This limit helps prevent abuse and denial-of-service attacks, and ensures that the API remains available for all users.
d14:b283.heading: Rate limits for the REST API > About primary rate limits
section_context: Rate limits for the REST API

d17:b283.text: The GitHub REST API is versioned. The API version name is based on the date when the API version was released. For example, the API version 2026-03-10 was released on Tue, 10 Mar 2026.
d17:b283.heading: API Versions > About API versioning

d17:b301.text: When a new REST API version is released, the previous API version will be supported for at least 24 more months following the release of the new API version.
d17:b301.heading: API Versions > About API versioning

d17:b308.text: Before upgrading to a new REST API version, you should read the changelog of breaking changes for the new API version to understand what breaking changes are included and to learn more about how to upgrade to that specific API version. For more information, see Breaking changes .
d17:b308.heading: API Versions > Upgrading to a new API version
section_context: Upgrading to a new API version

d17:b309.text: When you update your integration to specify the new API version in the X-GitHub-Api-Version header, you'll also need to make any changes required for your integration to work with the new API version.
d17:b309.heading: API Versions > Upgrading to a new API version
section_context: Upgrading to a new API version

d17:b318.text: Requests that do not specify an API version default to the next oldest supported version, not the closing down version. If you rely on unversioned requests, you may observe behavioral changes as older versions are removed from support.
d17:b318.heading: API Versions > API version closing down

d17:b330.text: You can also make an API request to get all of the supported API versions. For more information, see REST API endpoints for meta data .
d17:b330.heading: API Versions > Supported API versions

d17:b303.text: You should use the X-GitHub-Api-Version header to specify an API version. For example:
d17:b303.heading: API Versions > Specifying an API version

d17:b312.text: API versions are supported for 24 months after a newer API version is released.
d17:b312.heading: API Versions > API version closing down

d17:b323.text: Critical security vulnerabilities, data exposure risks, or severe reliability issues may require changes outside the normal release schedule. GitHub may release an unscheduled API version, backport fixes to supported versions, or in rare cases, introduce a breaking change to an existing version to protect users and platform integrity.
d17:b323.heading: API Versions > Exceptions to standard versioning > Security, availability, and reliability issues

d17:b273.text: Learn how to specify which REST API version to use whenever you make a request to the REST API.
d17:b273.heading: API Versions

d17:b305.text: Requests without the X-GitHub-Api-Version header will default to use the 2022-11-28 version.
d17:b305.heading: API Versions > Specifying an API version

d17:b328.text: The following REST API versions are currently supported.
d17:b328.heading: API Versions > Supported API versions

d17:b284.text: Breaking changes are changes that can potentially break an integration. Breaking changes will be released in a new API version. We will provide advance notice before releasing breaking changes. Breaking changes include:
d17:b284.heading: API Versions > About API versioning

d17:b294.text: Any additive (non-breaking) changes will be available in all supported API versions. Additive changes are changes that should not break an integration. Additive changes include:
d17:b294.heading: API Versions > About API versioning

d17:b306.text: If you specify an API version that is no longer supported, you will receive a 410 Gone response.
d17:b306.heading: API Versions > Specifying an API version

d17:b310.text: Once your integration is updated, test your integration to verify that it works with the new API version.
d17:b310.heading: API Versions > Upgrading to a new API version
section_context: Upgrading to a new API version

d17:b313.text: While a version is within its support window but approaching closing down, GitHub includes the following headers in API responses to help you prepare for migration:
d17:b313.heading: API Versions > API version closing down

d17:b314.text: Deprecation — The date when the API version will be closing down, formatted as an HTTP date per RFC 7231 . For example: Wed, 27 Nov 2019 14:34:29 GMT .
d17:b314.heading: API Versions > API version closing down

d17:b315.text: Sunset — The date when the API version will be completely removed (retired), after which requests will return a 410 Gone response. Follows RFC 8594 . For example: Fri, 27 Nov 2020 14:34:29 GMT .
d17:b315.heading: API Versions > API version closing down

d17:b317.text: Requests that specify a closing down API version receive a 410 Gone response.
d17:b317.heading: API Versions > API version closing down

d17:b319.text: For more information on migrating to a newer API version, see Breaking changes .
d17:b319.heading: API Versions > API version closing down

d17:b321.text: In rare cases, GitHub may make changes outside the normal API versioning cadence. These are exceptional interventions that do not alter the standard versioning guarantees for most integrators.
d17:b321.heading: API Versions > Exceptions to standard versioning

d17:b329.text: API version End of support date 2026-03-10 Not yet scheduled 2022-11-28 March 10, 2028
d17:b329.heading: API Versions > Supported API versions

d17:b324.text: GitHub will communicate such changes through release notes, changelogs, and direct communication explaining what changed and why. Where feasible, advance notice will be provided. Immediate action may be taken without advance notice when required.
d17:b324.heading: API Versions > Exceptions to standard versioning > Security, availability, and reliability issues

d19:b290.text: Because REST APIs have been around for longer than GraphQL APIs, some developers are more comfortable with the REST API. Since REST APIs use standard HTTP verbs and concepts, many developers are already familiar with the basic concepts to use the REST API.
d19:b290.heading: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API > Choosing the REST API
section_context: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API

d19:b284.text: The GraphQL API returns exactly the data that you request. GraphQL also returns the data in a pre-known structure based on your request. In contrast, the REST API returns more data than you requested and returns it in a pre-determined structure. You can also accomplish the equivalent of multiple REST API request in a single GraphQL request. The ability to make fewer requests and fetch less data makes GraphQL appealing to developers of mobile applications.
d19:b284.heading: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API > Choosing the GraphQL API
section_context: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API

d19:b282.text: This article discusses the benefits of each API. For more information about the GraphQL API, see About the GraphQL API . For more information about the REST API, see About the REST API .
d19:b282.heading: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API > About GitHub's APIs
section_context: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API

d19:b280.text: GitHub provides two APIs: a REST API and a GraphQL API. You can interact with both APIs using GitHub CLI, curl, the official Octokit libraries, and third party libraries. Occasionally, a feature may be supported on one API but not the other.
d19:b280.heading: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API > About GitHub's APIs
section_context: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API

d19:b281.text: You should use the API that best aligns with your needs and that you are most comfortable using. You don't need to exclusively use one API over the other. Node IDs let you move between the REST API and GraphQL API. For more information, see Using global node IDs .
d19:b281.heading: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API > About GitHub's APIs
section_context: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API

d19:b288.text: In contrast, to get this same information from the REST API, you would need to first make a request to GET /user/followers . The API would return the login of each follower, along with other data about the followers that you don't need. Then, for each follower, you would need to make a request to GET /users/{username}/followers . In total, you would need to make 11 requests to get the same information that you could get from a single GraphQL request, and you would receive excess data.
d19:b288.heading: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API > Choosing the GraphQL API
section_context: Comparing GitHub's REST API and GraphQL API

d19:b293.text: In contrast, to make an issue using the GraphQL API, you would need to get the node ID of the octocat/Spoon-Knife repository and then send a request like:

d19:b285.text: For example, to get the GitHub login of ten of your followers, and the login of ten followers of each of your followers, you can send a single request like:

d19:b286.text: { viewer { followers ( first : 10 ) { nodes { login followers ( first : 10 ) { nodes { login } } } } } }

d7:b158.text: To test and gradually roll out support for expiring tokens, you can opt in to receive an expiring token and a refresh token for an individual sign-in by requesting the offline_access scope in addition to your other scopes. When you request the offline_access scope, you will receive an expiring access token and a refresh token even if your app is not configured to use expiring tokens.
d7:b158.heading: Authorizing OAuth apps > Expiring access tokens > Opting in to expiring tokens at runtime

d7:b242.text: The scopes on the new access token will match the scopes of the previous token. You cannot provide a scope parameter during token refresh in order to change the access of the resulting token.

d7:b262.text: There is a limit of ten tokens that are issued per user/application/scope combination, and a rate limit of ten tokens created per hour. If an application creates more than ten tokens for the same user and the same scopes, GitHub revokes one of the existing tokens with the same user/application/scope combination, chosen in this order:
d7:b262.heading: Authorizing OAuth apps > Creating multiple tokens for OAuth apps
section_context: Creating multiple tokens for OAuth apps

d7:b156.text: The access token expires after eight hours, and the refresh token expires after six months without use. You can use the refresh token to generate a new access token and a new refresh token. For more information, see Refreshing an access token with a refresh token .

d8:b167.text: Also, since there's a hierarchical relationship between scopes, you should check if you were granted any higher levels of the required scope. For example, if the application had asked for user scope, it won't have been granted explicitly the user:email scope. In that case, it would receive a token with the user scope, which would work for requesting the user's email address, even though it doesn't explicitly include user:email on the token. Checking for both user and user:email ensures that you check for both scenarios.
d8:b167.heading: Authenticating to the REST API with an OAuth app > Accepting user authorization > Checking granted scopes
section_context: Authenticating to the REST API with an OAuth app

d8:b165.text: get '/callback' do # ... # Get the access_token using the code sample above # ... # check if we were granted user:email scope scopes = JSON .parse(result)[ 'scope' ].split( ',' ) has_user_email_scope = scopes. include ? 'user:email' | | scopes. include ? 'user' end
d8:b165.heading: Authenticating to the REST API with an OAuth app > Accepting user authorization > Checking granted scopes
section_context: Authenticating to the REST API with an OAuth app

d8:b154.text: Also, notice that the URL uses the scope query parameter to define the scopes requested by the application. For our application, we're requesting user:email scope for reading private email addresses. We'll also request the offline_access scope to get expiring tokens, which are better for security.
d8:b154.heading: Authenticating to the REST API with an OAuth app > Accepting user authorization
section_context: Authenticating to the REST API with an OAuth app

d8:b166.text: In our application, we're using scopes.include? to check if we were granted the user:email scope needed for fetching the authenticated user's private email addresses. Had the application asked for other scopes, we would have checked for those as well.
d8:b166.heading: Authenticating to the REST API with an OAuth app > Accepting user authorization > Checking granted scopes

d0:b171.text: A service account lets you manage permissions and create access tokens that authenticate API requests. Each service account has a client ID and a rotatable secret that function as a username and a password for creating access tokens. To learn how to construct an API request with an access token, see Make an API Request.
d0:b171.heading: Note

d0:b179.text: Atlas roles limit which operations a service account can authenticate with its access token. You must assign roles to service accounts as you would for users to ensure that the service account generates access tokens with the necessary permissions for the desired API calls.
d0:b179.heading: Tip > Service Account Token Best Practices

d0:b187.text: API keys have two parts: a Public Key and a Private Key. These serve the same function as a username and a password to authenticate API requests. To learn how to construct an API request using API keys, see Make an API Request.
d0:b187.heading: Important

d0:b158.text: We recommend you use service accounts instead of API keys to authenticate to the Atlas Administration API. API keys are a legacy authentication method.
d0:b158.heading: Important

d0:b176.text: Generate new tokens when needed : While you can't refresh an access token, you can generate a new token when your current token is close to expiry. This prevents service interruptions and allows you to maintain authorized service account access.
d0:b176.heading: Tip > Service Account Token Best Practices

d0:b185.text: We recommend you use service accounts instead of API keys to authenticate to the Atlas Administration API. API keys are a legacy authentication method.
d0:b185.heading: Important

d0:b191.text: Atlas roles limit which operations API keys can perform. You must assign roles to API keys as you would for users to ensure the API keys have the necessary permissions for the desired API calls.
d0:b191.heading: Important

d0:b165.text: Many Atlas Administration API endpoint URLs follow the format of /api/atlas/<version>/groups/<GROUP-ID>/ , where <GROUP-ID> is your project ID . For these resources, the service account or API keys that you use to authenticate the request must be a member of the organization that hosts the project. Otherwise, Atlas responds with a 401
d0:b165.heading: Note

d0:b169.text: Service accounts are the recommended method to manage authentication to the Atlas Administration API. Service accounts provide improved security over API keys by using the industry standard OAuth 2.0
d0:b169.heading: Note

d0:b175.text: Reuse tokens : Service account access tokens have a 1 hour (3600 seconds) lifespan, during which you can reuse the token multiple times. Avoid creating new tokens for every request.
d0:b175.heading: Tip > Service Account Token Best Practices

d0:b177.text: Revoke unnecessary tokens : When you no longer need a token, revoke the token's access to minimize security risks and ensure that only active tokens have access to your service account.
d0:b177.heading: Tip > Service Account Token Best Practices

d1:b157.text: The Atlas Go SDK provides platform-specific and Go language-specific tools, libraries, and documentation to help you build applications that interact with Atlas quickly and easily using the Atlas Administration API.
d1:b157.heading: Tip

d1:b176.text: CDK for Terraform leverages the MongoDB Atlas Atlas Administration API to enable provisioning across popular programming languages such as JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, Go, and C#. Utilizing the powerful capabilities of Terraform, with CDKTF you can now create, manage, and update your Atlas resources with ease and deploy them seamlessly in the cloud without context switching from the native programming language of choice.
d1:b176.heading: Tip

d1:b148.text: You can interact with Atlas programmatically to perform administrative tasks or manage your deployments using the following resources.

d1:b165.text: The Atlas CLI is a command-line interface built specifically for MongoDB Atlas . You can use Atlas CLI to interact with Atlas from the terminal with short and intuitive commands and accomplish complex operational tasks such as creating a cluster or setting up an access list interactively and programmatically.
d1:b165.heading: Tip

d1:b170.text: HashiCorp Terraform MongoDB Atlas Provider provides refined programmatic access and management of MongoDB Atlas resources. You can define your environment using the HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) and deploy, update, and manage Atlas infrastructure as code through HashiCorp Terraform. This allows you to integrate Atlas into your continuous delivery workflows.
d1:b170.heading: Tip

d1:b182.text: Atlas CloudFormation Resources helps you to manage MongoDB Atlas . It simplifies provisioning and management of Atlas features on AWS . You can create YAML- or JSON-based templates for the service or application architectures you want and have AWS CloudFormation use those templates for quick and reliable provisioning of the services or applications (called "stacks"). You can also easily update or replicate the stacks as needed.
d1:b182.heading: Tip

d1:b187.text: AWS Partner Solutions provide pre-built CloudFormation templates to help you provision a group of Atlas resources for specific use cases instead of deploying them one by one. Partner Solutions help you deploy popular technologies to AWS according to AWS best practices.
d1:b187.heading: Tip

d1:b191.text: If you prefer using familiar programming languages like JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, and Go rather than using YAML or JSON , you can use the AWS CDK to deploy Atlas resources. When you execute your AWS CDK applications, they automatically generate CloudFormation templates, which in turn utilize the AWS CloudFormation service for resource provisioning. This way, you benefit from the abstraction and flexibility provided by AWS CDK and take advantage of the robustness of CloudFormation for infrastructure management, while still using the programming language of your choice.
d1:b191.heading: Tip

d1:b197.text: The Atlas Kubernetes Operator enables you to manage Atlas resources through custom resources that you apply in Kubernetes . This allows an infrastructure as code approach to manage declarative configuration for Atlas using a GitOps workflow, allowing developers to configure Atlas resources using the same process and tooling that they use to deploy application components into Kubernetes . The automatic creation of a Kubernetes secret containing the connection string for a database user simplifies the process of connecting an application to the database.
d1:b197.heading: Tip

d2:b188.text: IP access lists apply only to programmatic API keys and service accounts. They don't apply to other types of access to the Atlas Administration API, such as the Atlas CLI or delegated access granted through Atlas App Connections. Delegated access includes third-party partner applications, MongoDB applications such as MongoDB Compass , and Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients. If your organization requires all Atlas Administration API traffic to originate from specific addresses, don't enable delegated app access for that organization. Delegated access settings for partner applications and MCP clients are off by default in existing organizations.
d2:b188.heading: Note

d2:b203.text: If you haven't already created a service account or API keys for an organization, you can create them for a project to grant that project access to the Atlas Administration API. This limits API requests to only those from the location-based IP or CIDR addresses that you specify in the IP access list. d5:b196.text: If you cannot use built-in authentication methods, you can use callback authentication with any OAuth 2.0 authorization service. With callback authentication, the MongoDB driver calls a provided callback method to get a JWT token for database access. Within your callback method, retrieve the token from your authorization provider using your preferred mechanism, such as certificate authentication, client credentials flow, or an SDK.
d5:b196.heading: Note

d5:b165.text: Workload Identity Federation allows your applications access to MongoDB clusters with OAuth2.0 access tokens. The access tokens can be issued by any external Identity Provider including Azure Entra ID and Google Cloud Platform. Atlas stores the user identifiers and privileges, but not the secrets. This authentication mechanism for your applications is only supported by MongoDB drivers. Other MongoDB tools like mongosh and MongoDB Compass don't support this authentication mechanism.
d5:b165.heading: Note

d5:b259.text: The number 2 represents Version 2 of Microsoft's access tokens. Other applications can use this as a signed attestation of the Active Directory-managed user's identity. Version 2 ensures that the token is a JSON Web Token that MongoDB understands.
d5:b259.heading: Note

d5:b166.text: MongoDB Drivers support two types of authentication flow for Workload Identity Federation : Built-in Authentication and Callback Authentication.
d5:b166.heading: Note

d5:b197.text: To confirm that your chosen driver supports Workload Identity Federation authentication and review additional implementation details, see the list of driver versions that support Workload Identity Federation authentication.
d5:b197.heading: Note

d5:b205.text: Secure "Passwordless" Authentication: Your applications obtain short-lived OAuth 2.0 access tokens from the Azure metadata server, which MongoDB Atlas then verifies. This eliminates the need to store and manage sensitive database usernames and passwords within your application code or configurations.
d5:b205.heading: Note

d5:b317.text: Select Group Membership to grant authorization based on group membership, or select User ID to authorize an individual user.
d5:b317.heading: Note > Prerequisite

d5:b443.text: Don't use this feature to rotate your signing keys. When you rotate your Workload Identity Federation signing keys, MongoDB fetches the JWKS automatically upon expiration of the existing access tokens.
d5:b443.heading: Note

d5:b168.text: You can use built-in authentication if you deploy your application on a supported infrastructure with a supported principal type. Your application can access Atlas clusters without supplying a password or manually requesting a JWT from your cloud provider's metadata service. Instead, your chosen MongoDB driver uses your existing principal identifier to request a JWT access token under the hood, which is then passed to the Atlas cluster automatically when your application connects.
d5:b168.heading: Note

d5:b200.text: Azure Service Principals: Use the client-credentials flow or certificate authentication to retrieve the access token and grant access for applications.
d5:b200.heading: Note

d7:b187.text: API keys have two parts: a Public Key and a Private Key. These serve the same function as a username and a password to authenticate API requests. To learn how to construct an API request using API keys, see Make an API Request.

d7:b165.heading: Note

d7:b169.text: Service accounts are the recommended method to manage authentication to the Atlas Administration API. Service accounts provide improved security over API keys by using the industry standard OAuth 2.0
d7:b169.heading: Note

d7:b175.text: Reuse tokens : Service account access tokens have a 1 hour (3600 seconds) lifespan, during which you can reuse the token multiple times. Avoid creating new tokens for every request.
d7:b175.heading: Tip > Service Account Token Best Practices

d7:b177.text: Revoke unnecessary tokens : When you no longer need a token, revoke the token's access to minimize security risks and ensure that only active tokens have access to your service account.
d7:b177.heading: Tip > Service Account Token Best Practices

d12:b148.text: You can interact with Atlas programmatically to perform administrative tasks or manage your deployments using the following resources.

d12:b165.text: The Atlas CLI is a command-line interface built specifically for MongoDB Atlas . You can use Atlas CLI to interact with Atlas from the terminal with short and intuitive commands and accomplish complex operational tasks such as creating a cluster or setting up an access list interactively and programmatically.
d12:b165.heading: Tip

d12:b170.text: HashiCorp Terraform MongoDB Atlas Provider provides refined programmatic access and management of MongoDB Atlas resources. You can define your environment using the HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) and deploy, update, and manage Atlas infrastructure as code through HashiCorp Terraform. This allows you to integrate Atlas into your continuous delivery workflows.
d12:b170.heading: Tip

d12:b182.text: Atlas CloudFormation Resources helps you to manage MongoDB Atlas . It simplifies provisioning and management of Atlas features on AWS . You can create YAML- or JSON-based templates for the service or application architectures you want and have AWS CloudFormation use those templates for quick and reliable provisioning of the services or applications (called "stacks"). You can also easily update or replicate the stacks as needed.
d12:b182.heading: Tip

d12:b187.text: AWS Partner Solutions provide pre-built CloudFormation templates to help you provision a group of Atlas resources for specific use cases instead of deploying them one by one. Partner Solutions help you deploy popular technologies to AWS according to AWS best practices.
d12:b187.heading: Tip

d12:b191.text: If you prefer using familiar programming languages like JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, and Go rather than using YAML or JSON , you can use the AWS CDK to deploy Atlas resources. When you execute your AWS CDK applications, they automatically generate CloudFormation templates, which in turn utilize the AWS CloudFormation service for resource provisioning. This way, you benefit from the abstraction and flexibility provided by AWS CDK and take advantage of the robustness of CloudFormation for infrastructure management, while still using the programming language of your choice.
d12:b191.heading: Tip

d12:b197.text: The Atlas Kubernetes Operator enables you to manage Atlas resources through custom resources that you apply in Kubernetes . This allows an infrastructure as code approach to manage declarative configuration for Atlas using a GitOps workflow, allowing developers to configure Atlas resources using the same process and tooling that they use to deploy application components into Kubernetes . The automatic creation of a Kubernetes secret containing the connection string for a database user simplifies the process of connecting an application to the database.
d12:b197.heading: Tip

d17:b160.text: MCP Host : Application or environment where you want to use MCP, such as a chat interface or IDE. For example, Claude Desktop or VS Code.

d17:b162.text: MCP Servers : Programs that expose specific capabilities to the client. For example, the MongoDB MCP Server.

d17:b168.text: The MongoDB MCP Server is our official MCP server implementation that gives your AI client a set of tools that can be used to interact with your MongoDB data and deployments. These tools include various administrative actions, such as managing cluster resources, database operations like querying and indexing, and performance optimization through the Performance Advisor.

d17:b174.text: Manual configuration file setup : You manually add the MongoDB MCP Server configuration and your OAuth client credentials to a configuration file for your AI client. This setup path is best for working with programmatic agents. Programmatic agents are automated, workflow-driven agents that can run multi-step workflows without a user's input or guidance.

d17:b180.text: MongoDB hosts, runs, and maintains the MongoDB MCP Server in Atlas. There is no MCP server infrastructure for you to deploy, upgrade, or operate.

d17:b198.text: Use Local MCP when you want direct control over how and where the MCP server runs. In exchange for this control, you take on hosting and maintaining the server, including server upgrades and credential management.

d17:b199.text: You also use Local MCP when you want to use the MongoDB MCP Server with local deployment types, such as MongoDB Atlas Local, MongoDB Community Edition, and MongoDB Enterprise Advanced.

d0:b94.text: Linear hosts images and other assets uploaded into Linear behind authentication. Only authenticated users can view their assets. This also applies to the API and all images will require authentication to be displayed outside Linear’s application. Regular API authentication (OAuth or API keys) is accepted for displaying images. d0:b67.text: Linear’s GraphQL API follows the standard GraphQL error format, returning errors within an errors array in the response. Each error object includes a message describing what went wrong, a path array indicating where in the query the error occurred, and extensions that may contain additional context such as error codes or validation details.
d0:b67.heading: Getting started

d0:b68.text: Always check for the errors array before assuming success—GraphQL queries can partially succeed with a 200 HTTP status, returning some data while including errors for failed fields. Monitor HTTP status codes for server errors (5xx) and make sure to correctly handle rate limits . Use strongly-typed GraphQL clients when possible to catch validation errors at development time, and always validate required fields to avoid runtime null value errors.
d0:b68.heading: Getting started

d0:b70.text: The Linear SDK exposes the Linear GraphQL schema, and makes it easy to access models, or perform mutations. We recommend using it to interact with the GraphQL API. It is written in TypeScript, allowing all operations to be strongly typed.

d0:b73.text: Our GraphQL API is explorable and queryable via Apollo Studio , no download or log in required. Click the Schema tab to browse the schema, and click the Explorer tab to run queries.

d0:b78.text: As issues (and most other objects) are team based, you first need to get the ID of the team you want to interact with:

d0:b80.text: Once you have found the correct team, you can get the issues for that team. Lets make a request with also some other issue metadata:
d0:b80.heading: Getting started

d0:b81.text: query Team { team(id: "9cfb482a-81e3-4154-b5b9-2c805e70a02d") { id name issues { nodes { id title description assignee { id name } createdAt archivedAt } } } }
d0:b81.heading: Getting started

d0:b82.text: We can also get an issue by id:
d0:b82.heading: Getting started

d0:b83.text: query Issue { issue(id: "BLA-123") { id title description } }
d0:b83.heading: Getting started

d0:b84.text: Locate the IDs of teams, issues and other entities directly within Linear itself from the command menu: Cmd/Ctrl+K and “Copy model UUID”. This will show results based on the page you’re currently viewing within Linear.

d0:b86.text: To create a new issue, use a mutation:
d0:b86.heading: Getting started

d0:b87.text: mutation IssueCreate { issueCreate( input: { title: "New exception" description: "More detailed error report in markdown" teamId: "9cfb482a-81e3-4154-b5b9-2c805e70a02d" } ) { success issue { id title } } }
d0:b87.heading: Getting started

d0:b88.text: This mutation will create a new issue and return its id and title if the call was successful ( success: true ).
d0:b88.heading: Getting started

d0:b89.text: If an issue is created without a specified stateId (the status field for the issue), the issue will be assigned to the team’s first state in the Backlog workflow state category. If the “Triage” feature is turned on for the team, then the issue will be assigned to the Triage workflow state.
d0:b89.heading: Getting started

d0:b90.text: A common use case after creating an issue is updating the issue. To do this we can use the issueUpdate mutation, using the input field to include whatever it is we want to change. The id provided can be either be the uuid returned by the creation query, or the shorthand id like BLA-123 below.
d0:b90.heading: Getting started

d0:b91.text: mutation IssueUpdate { issueUpdate( id: "BLA-123", input: { title: "New Issue Title" stateId: "NEW-STATE-ID", } ) { success issue { id title state { id name } } } }
d0:b91.heading: Getting started

d0:b92.text: Changes made to an issue’s properties in the first 3 minutes are considered part of the issue creation process, and won’t be added to the activity log as changes to the issue.

d2:b89.text: Once installed and authenticated, your agent is ready to interact in the workspace. The core interaction model centers around the Agent Session , which tracks the lifecycle of a given agent task. Sessions are created automatically when an agent is mentioned or delegated an issue.
d2:b89.heading: Getting Started

d2:b90.text: Session state is visible to users, and updated automatically based on the agent’s emitted activities. No manual state management is required.
d2:b90.heading: Getting Started

d2:b52.text: This guide describes how to best integrate an AI agent into Linear. It includes implementation guidelines on how to design an experience that feels native to Linear’s workflows and interaction patterns.
d2:b52.heading: Getting Started

d2:b56.text: Agents behave similar to other users in a workspace. They can be @mentioned, delegated issues through assignment, create and reply to comments, collaborate on projects and documents, etc. App users are installed and managed by workspace admins.
d2:b56.heading: Getting Started

d2:b57.text: You can build agents for internal use within your own workspace or for distribution to other organizations. It does not cost anything to develop agents in Linear. To make your agent available to other workspaces, submit your agent to Linear’s integration directory.
d2:b57.heading: Getting Started

d2:b58.text: Additionally, agents installed in your workspace do not count as billable users.
d2:b58.heading: Getting Started

d2:b59.text: We’ve created a demo agent built on our Typescript SDK and Cloudflare, if you want to dive straight into an example codebase.
d2:b59.heading: Getting Started

d2:b60.text: Weather Bot is an agent that will help you look up the weather of any location within a Linear issue.
d2:b60.heading: Getting Started

d2:b63.text: In the configuration, enable webhooks and make sure to select Agent session events at the bottom. Enabling this category will notify your webhook when events occur that are directly relevant to your app’s user.
d2:b63.heading: Getting Started

d2:b64.text: Note that the name and icon of your application will be how the agent appears in workspaces where it is installed (e.g. in the mention and filter menus), so it is best to choose something short, recognizable, but unique.
d2:b64.heading: Getting Started

d2:b73.text: Assigning an issue to your app now sets it as the delegate , not the assignee —so humans maintain ownership while agents act on their behalf.
d2:b73.heading: Getting Started

d2:b92.text: The most common entry point is delegation—when a user assigns an issue to your agent.
d2:b92.heading: Getting Started

d2:b93.text: This triggers a created AgentSessionEvent webhook containing an agentSession object with the relevant issue, comment, and context.

d2:b95.text: Emit a thought activity within 10 seconds to acknowledge the session has begun

d2:b96.text: Use the promptContext field to construct a formatted string containing the session’s relevant context, such as issue details, comments, and guidance
d2:b96.heading: Getting Started

d3:b51.text: Login restrictions are available to workspaces on our Business and Enterprise plans. SAML authentication and IP restrictions are only available to workspaces on our Enterprise plan.
d3:b51.heading: Login methods

d3:b61.text: Passkeys allow a secure and fast login without having to rely on passwords. They are supported by all major browsers, mobile operating systems, and many password managers like 1Password. You can register multiple devices to log in via passkey from Preferences > Account > Security & Access .
d3:b61.heading: Login methods

d3:b71.text: You can log in to multiple user accounts in Linear, which allows you to switch between workspaces associated with those accounts without re-authenticating. To add a user account:
d3:b71.heading: Login methods

d3:b56.text: Members can authenticate with Linear using Google authentication when using a Google supported email address.
d3:b56.heading: Login methods

d3:b67.text: IP restrictions are available only on the Enterprise plan.
d3:b67.heading: Login methods

d3:b68.text: Workspace access can be restricted to specific IPs to enable an extra security layer for accessing Linear. Once set, direct user access to the workspace, including web, desktop, and mobile access, will be limited to the set of configured IPs. Access can be restricted to one or more IP addresses or ranges, specified using CIDR notation.
d3:b68.heading: Login methods

d3:b50.text: We offer multiple ways to log in and options to restrict login methods for added security.
d3:b50.heading: Login methods

d3:b53.text: Linear provides several options for members to log into a workspace and allows for different tiers of restriction methods for added security.
d3:b53.heading: Login methods

d3:b65.text: Admins can require specific login methods for all members. This setting can be managed by navigating to Settings > Administration > Security . Users with the highest role in the workspace (owners or admins, depending on the workspace) can login through any method to ensure they have access to these settings and prevent lockouts for other users.
d3:b65.heading: Login methods

d3:b69.text: To configure IP restrictions, go to Settings > Administration > Security .
d3:b69.heading: Login methods

d3:b79.text: Once authenticated, you will be directed to the last visited workspace for that email address.
d3:b79.heading: Login methods

d3:b85.text: Click on your workspace name in the top left and check that you are logged into all accounts. If you see a number next to Create or join a workspace , it’s possible you’ve have a pending workspace invite and can accept this to join. If you’re still having difficulty, please reach out to support@linear.app.
d3:b85.heading: Login methods

d3:b58.text: When selecting Continue with Email as the login option, an email will be sent to your inbox containing a login link. You can either use the link to log in or copy the code provided in the email and paste it into the “Enter code” field on the login page.
d3:b58.heading: Login methods

d3:b59.text: We recommend whitelisting notifications@linear.app and/or pm_bounces@pm-bounces.linear.app as trusted senders in your email settings to ensure login emails reach your inbox.
d3:b59.heading: Login methods

d3:b63.text: Refer to our SAML help docs.
d3:b63.heading: Login methods

d3:b72.text: Click on your workspace name in the top left corner to launch a dropdown
d3:b72.heading: Login methods

d3:b74.text: Select Create or join a workspace .
d3:b74.heading: Login methods

d3:b75.text: (Optional) Follow the prompts to create a new workspace.
d3:b75.heading: Login methods

d3:b76.text: If you have an existing workspace under a different email address, click your existing email address in the upper-right corner.
d3:b76.heading: Login methods

d3:b80.text: If you click the workspace name in the upper left and hover over Switch workspace , you will see all the other workspaces associated with the added email in the list of options.
d3:b80.heading: Login methods

d3:b82.text: For security purposes, when signing out of a workspace in a given location, you will be signed out of all other sessions, requiring you to log back in next time you access Linear elsewhere.
d3:b82.heading: Login methods

d4:b184.text: OAuth2 apps can have up to 1000 active client credentials tokens in parallel, provided each token uses the same scopes. If you request a client credentials token with different scopes, all existing app actor tokens for the app are revoked and replaced with the new token carrying the updated scopes. If you first generate an app actor token via a different grant type, you will not be able to hold multiple app tokens in parallel—all app tokens must be generated via client credentials if you want multiple active ones.
d4:b184.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b94.text: GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URL&state=SECURE_RANDOM&scope=read HTTP/1.1 GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?client_id=client1&redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A3000%2Foauth%2Fcallback&response_type=code&scope=read,write HTTP/1.1 GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?client_id=client1&redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A3000%2Foauth%2Fcallback&response_type=code&scope=read,write&code_challenge=challenge&code_challenge_method=S256 HTTP/1.1
d4:b94.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b231.text: GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URL&state=SECURE_RANDOM&scope=read HTTP / 1.1 GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?client_id=client1&redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A3000%2Foauth%2Fcallback&response_type=code&scope=read,write HTTP / 1.1 GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?client_id=client1&redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A3000%2Foauth%2Fcallback&response_type=code&scope=read,write&code_challenge=challenge&code_challenge_method=S256 HTTP / 1.1
d4:b231.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b167.text: Note: For backwards compatibility, we still accept revocation via the Authorization header or the legacy access_token / refresh_token form fields. New integrations should use the token field. The token field must not be combined with legacy fields.
d4:b167.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b183.text: The app user’s team access can be modified through the app details page for your app at any point after the token is generated. Since there is no refresh token paired with this access token, your server is expected to fetch a new token if it receives a 401 error when making a request with the previous token.
d4:b183.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b159.text: Once you have obtained a valid access token, you can make a request to Linear’s GraphQL API. You can initialize the Linear Client with the access token:

d4:b161.text: Or pass the token as an authorization header: Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>

d4:b162.text: curl https://api.linear.app/graphql \ -X POST \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>' \ --data '{ "query": "{ viewer { id name } }" }' \
d4:b162.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b165.text: If available, include token_type_hint ( access_token or refresh_token ) to help the server identify the token.
d4:b165.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b179.text: We support the client_credentials grant type for OAuth2 apps that use tokens for server-to-server communication and cannot support a user-initiated OAuth flow involving refresh tokens.
d4:b179.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b180.text: Request a new client credentials token at the start of each run, then use it only for that run. Do not manually copy or persist an access token as a long-lived API key.
d4:b180.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b245.text: curl https://api.linear.app/graphql \ -X POST \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>' \ --data '{ "query": "{ viewer { id name } }" }' \

d4:b54.text: All OAuth2 applications were migrated to the new refresh token system on April 1, 2026. Specifically for CI and scheduled automation, refer to Client credentials token .
d4:b54.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b133.text: After a successful request, a valid access token and refresh token will be returned in the response. The access token is valid for 24 hours and will need to be refreshed when it expires. Example response:
d4:b133.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b135.text: Note: OAuth apps created prior to Dec 1, 2023 will instead return scope as an array of strings in the token response.
d4:b135.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b137.text: You’ll need to use the refresh token you receive alongside your access token to retrieve a new access token when the previous one expires.
d4:b137.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b139.text: Use HTTP basic authentication by passing a Base64-encoded client_id:client_secret string as an authorization header: Authorization: Basic <base64(client_id:client_secret)>
d4:b139.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b142.text: Requests to consume a refresh token and obtain a new one have a 30-minute grace period to allow for network errors. If you make a request with a valid refresh token but do not receive the new one in the response, you can replay the original request to retrieve the new refresh token up to 30 minutes after the original request.
d4:b142.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b176.text: Rotating your client secret immediately invalidates any client credentials tokens issued for your application. It does not revoke access or refresh tokens already granted to individual workspaces — those keep working, and will use your new secret the next time they’re refreshed. If you need to revoke those as well, do so separately (see “Revoking access tokens” above).
d4:b176.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b182.text: The token generated using this grant type will be an app actor token that has access to all public teams in the workspace and is valid for 30 days. You can learn more about app actor tokens here .
d4:b182.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d4:b188.text: Use HTTP basic authentication by passing a Base64-encoded client_id:client_secret string as an authorization header: Authorization: Basic <base64(client_id:client_secret)>
d4:b188.heading: OAuth 2.0 authentication

d6:b51.text: Available to workspaces on any paid plan.
d6:b51.heading: Third-Party App Approvals

d6:b53.text: Requiring approval for third-party applications ensures that the people with permission to manage apps control which applications can access the workspace and its data.
d6:b53.heading: Third-Party App Approvals

d6:b55.text: Third-party application approvals are available on any paid plan.
d6:b55.heading: Third-Party App Approvals

d6:b50.text: Enable third-party application approvals for your workspace to maintain control over which applications can be installed.
d6:b50.heading: Third-Party App Approvals

d6:b56.text: A workspace owner in an Enterprise workspace—or a workspace admin in any other paid workspace—can turn on third-party application approvals from Settings > Administration > Security .
d6:b56.heading: Third-Party App Approvals

d6:b59.text: When a workspace member tries to install a third-party app, Linear will display a screen which allows the member to request approval and optionally include a reason for their request. If the application has already been denied previously, Linear will let the requestor know and share the reason.
d6:b59.heading: Third-Party App Approvals

d6:b61.text: Workspace owners in Enterprise workspaces—and workspace admins in all other paid workspaces—will receive an email and an in-app notification when an application has been requested for approval. This notification will contain a link to the workspace applications page so you can approve or deny the application swiftly. Once the application has been approved or denied, the member who requested the application will also receive an email and an in-app notification. When denying a request, they can include an optional reason. This reason will be shared with the member who made the request.
d6:b61.heading: Third-Party App Approvals

d7:b560.text: Enterprise-managed Authorization lets Okta administrators manage access and permissions centrally, and users automatically get access to the MCP servers they’re authorized to use when they sign in to Claude.
d7:b560.heading: Now > Initiative properties

d7:b247.text: For work that requires tighter access, initiatives led by private teams are only visible to team members. This creates a secure place for confidential planning, regulated projects, audits, and other restricted work.
d7:b247.heading: Now > Team initiatives

d7:b438.text: When editing, changes you make through Linear Agent highlight separately so they’re easy to review. If you need to revert to an earlier version, restore to any previous checkpoint from version history.
d7:b438.heading: Now > Text attribution and agent-assisted editing

d7:b561.text: Enterprise-Managed Authorization is available to Enterprise workspaces using Okta as an identity provider and Claude as an MCP client. Learn more in the docs or in the MCP specification .
d7:b561.heading: Now > Initiative properties

d7:b35.text: In addition to creating issues and updating projects and initiatives, Loops can now edit documents. When scope or timing changes, a loop can update the relevant Linear document so plans stay aligned.
d7:b35.heading: Now > Loops for product management

d7:b167.text: Added CSV exports to workspace teams, team members, API keys, and usage history tables
d7:b167.heading: Now > Priority inbox

d7:b251.text: When employees connect from a supported Anthropic agent, Linear verifies their identity through Okta and applies their existing Linear permissions. Admins can manage access centrally, without requiring employees to sign in or authorize Linear individually.
d7:b251.heading: Now > Team initiatives

d7:b536.heading: Now > Introducing Loops

d7:b557.text: Use these properties to group and filter initiatives on any plan, or build custom initiative views on Enterprise plans. Learn more about initiative properties in the docs .

d7:b747.heading: Now > Agent assisted project updates

d7:b846.text: Earlier this year, we launched Linear Agent , giving teams a new way to plan and coordinate their issues and projects. Since then, we’ve added Code Intelligence to extend that understanding to the codebase, and MCP support to bring all of your context together.
d7:b846.heading: Now > Coding sessions in Linear

d7:b858.text: Coding sessions are available on Basic, Business, and Enterprise plans. They require a GitHub connection with code access and use AI credits to run. Workspace admins can enable coding sessions in Settings and manage access, usage, and credits from the usage dashboard. Learn more in the docs .
d7:b858.heading: Now > Coding sessions in Linear

d7:b27.text: Teams change project plans all the time. It’s not the change itself that’s hard, but the follow-through: updating docs, creating issues, and keeping everyone informed. That’s where information falls out of sync and handoffs get missed. Loops can now handle that coordination for you.
d7:b27.heading: Now > Loops for product management

d7:b28.text: For example, when a project’s target date changes, a loop can automatically update the launch plan and post a Slack message explaining what changed, why, and who needs to act.
d7:b28.heading: Now > Loops for product management

d7:b56.text: Updated Datadog MCP connections to use the supported v1 endpoints
d7:b56.heading: Now > Loops for product management

d7:b93.text: The new project composer lets you develop ideas with Linear Agent before creating a live project. Inside the composer, Linear can pull in relevant context from your workspace and connected tools to sharpen the brief and build out a plan.
d7:b93.heading: Now > Priority inbox

d7:b97.text: Document creation and editing are now available in Linear’s iOS and Android apps. Start a doc while the context is fresh, update a plan as it changes, or fix a detail before it sends someone in the wrong direction, without waiting until you’re back at your desk.
d7:b97.heading: Now > Priority inbox

d7:b102.text: As more apps and agents connect to your workspace, admins need control over which ones can access company data. Third-party app approvals are now available on paid Linear plans, allowing admins to review and approve apps before they’re installed.
d7:b102.heading: Now > Priority inbox

d7:b106.text: Fixed triage suggestions now showing the team name instead of the key
d7:b106.heading: Now > Priority inbox

d7:b193.text: During a session, Linear detects and installs the toolchains and dependencies it needs to complete the task. Teams can go further by pinning runtime versions, adding setup scripts, and defining environment variables.

d9:b50.text: We offer a free plan and different paid plans to suit your needs.

d9:b90.text: Workspace admins can change or cancel a subscription from Settings > Administration > Billing . Subscription updates take effect at the end of the subscription period . If you are on a monthly plan, this will be at the end of the billing month. If you are on a yearly plan, this will be at the end of the billing year.
d9:b90.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b51.text: Please see Pricing for rates and a feature-by-feature comparison by plan.
d9:b51.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b52.text: How our plans and billing works ⁠
d9:b52.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b54.text: Refer to our pricing page for the most up-to-date information on our plans offering.
d9:b54.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b56.text: Customers are billed for the number of unsuspended users within a workspace. Thus, your paid plan only applies to the single workspace associated with it.
d9:b56.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b57.text: For billing frequency, we offer either monthly or yearly options. On our Enterprise plan, we exclusively offer a yearly option.
d9:b57.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b60.text: Your account is charged on a monthly basis for the number of unsuspended users in any role on your workspace.
d9:b60.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b62.text: When you upgrade to a yearly plan, Linear charges for the total number of unsuspended users in your workspace at that time. This establishes your subscription year and billing cycle.
d9:b62.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b63.text: If you add or suspend users during that year, your account automatically adjusts to reflect those changes:
d9:b63.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b67.text: Linear reconciles these adjustments on your monthly billing cycle , which is tied to your annual plan’s start date (not the calendar month).
d9:b67.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b71.text: Your annual plan starts on February 10 and renews the following year.
d9:b71.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b74.text: This ensures your account stays accurate and that all future prorations calculate correctly. Any new user changes are automatically included in your next billing cycle — no manual action or adjustments needed.
d9:b74.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b76.text: “Billing month” refers to your plan’s recurring monthly cycle, not the calendar month.
d9:b76.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b83.text: Navigate to Settings > Administration > Billing to access your plan information and make changes. From here, you can:
d9:b83.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b91.text: We do not provide refunds for cancellations mid-subscription. If you are uncertain you are ready to commit to a full year, we recommend starting on a monthly plan first. You can switch to yearly at a later date when you are ready to commit longer term and take advantage of the discounted rates.
d9:b91.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b95.text: Members will become Admins of the workspace, as all users are Admins on free plans.
d9:b95.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b100.text: In certain areas Linear is required to apply sales tax. The billing address you provide is used to determine whether tax must be applied, and if so the applicable rate.
d9:b100.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b127.text: Discounts apply to our Basic and Business paid plans.
d9:b127.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b138.text: We offer 75% off our Basic and Business paid plans only (not available on Enterprise) to eligible charities (otherwise known as non-profits). Please reach out to us at support@linear.app to apply and provide proof of non-profit status.
d9:b138.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b145.text: A hospital, an organisation involved with health insurance or group health plans or a related organisation
d9:b145.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b149.text: The Linear for Startups program is designed to help early-stage startups discover a better, faster way to build and ship great products. Startups affiliated with a partner in Linear’s Startup Program receive up to 6 months of free access to Linear’s Business plan. For more information, visit https://linear.app/startups .
d9:b149.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b61.text: Adding users mid-month will not result in a charge until the following month. Similarly, removing a user mid-month will not result in a credit for the remainder of the month.
d9:b61.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b64.text: Adding users → generates a pro-rated charge for the remaining time in your subscription year.
d9:b64.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b65.text: Suspending users → generates a pro-rated credit for the remaining time in your subscription year.
d9:b65.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b66.text: All adjustments are fully automated — there’s no need to request manual changes. Credits are automatically applied toward future invoices or renewals (they aren’t refunded).
d9:b66.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b68.text: If additional users were added during the past monthly billing cycle, a true-up invoice is created and charged automatically or sent by email.
d9:b68.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b69.text: If users were suspended, a credit is automatically issued and applied to future invoices.
d9:b69.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b72.text: Date Event Result February 10 Upgrade with 12 active users You’re charged for 12 users for the full subscription year (Feb 10 → Feb 10). April 18 Add 3 users Linear calculates a pro-rated charge for those 3 users covering Apr 18 → Feb 10 next year. This appears on your next monthly billing cycle (May 10). May 15 Suspend 2 users Linear calculates a pro-rated credit for those 2 users covering May 15 → Feb 10 next year. This credit appears on your next monthly billing cycle (June 10).
d9:b72.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b73.text: Each change — adding or suspending users — is billed or credited based on the exact date it happens. Invoices only ever reflect past activity, and we don’t edit or cancel them once issued.
d9:b73.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b77.text: Annual subscriptions are charged once for the base year, with automated monthly true-ups for user changes.
d9:b77.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b78.text: Invoices are final once issued. Future user changes are automatically included in upcoming invoices.
d9:b78.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b79.text: Credits are automatically applied to future charges or renewals.
d9:b79.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b81.text: You also have the option to add AI credits to your workspace to unlock some additional AI features - more information on this in our AI credits docs .
d9:b81.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b87.text: View billing history — past invoices and charges.
d9:b87.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b88.text: We will also show if a charge is failed or past due.
d9:b88.heading: Billing and plans

d9:b126.text: We also offer university staff and employees a 75% discount at qualifying academic institutions.

d9:b129.text: The Education Program is open to colleges and higher-level educational institutions. It isn’t available for business or commercial use.

d11:b27.text: Building this tool requires a team of talented individuals who care deeply about the quality of their work, no matter if it’s engineering, design, or customer support. We are looking for people who share our passion for software craftsmanship and getting even the smallest details right. If that sounds like you, please reach out and join us on our quest.
d11:b27.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > On a quest for quality

d11:b19.text: We are building a new species of product tool. Will you help us make it better?
d11:b19.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools

d11:b25.text: We believe that there is a lost art of building software. A craftsmanship that yields products of an exceptional, almost magical, quality.
d11:b25.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > On a quest for quality

d11:b26.text: It’s difficult to describe this quality with words and impossible to measure it in numbers, but you can feel it when it’s there. You know it when you experience it. To bring back this level of quality, we are building a tool that empowers product teams to do their best work. A tool with unparalleled speed, focus, and design.
d11:b26.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > On a quest for quality

d11:b50.text: Linear’s mission is to inspire and accelerate builders. To turn that ambition into reality, we operate based on a set of core principles that keep us focused.

d11:b54.text: Listen carefully and understand their problems.
d11:b54.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > How we think and work

d11:b55.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > How we think and work

d11:b56.text: Find and create good things. Know what needs to change to make it better.
d11:b56.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > How we think and work

d11:b59.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > How we think and work

d11:b60.text: Put care into the foundation. Don’t make it a future person’s problem.
d11:b60.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > How we think and work

d11:b62.text: Don’t fix every problem. Avoid adding unnecessary process or documents.
d11:b62.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > How we think and work

d11:b63.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > How we think and work

d11:b64.text: Get to the point and assume good intentions.
d11:b64.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > How we think and work

d11:b65.text: 08 . Keep the team small, do more with less
d11:b65.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > How we think and work

d11:b66.text: We build better with fewer people. Wear multiple hats.

d11:b67.heading: Help us craft high-quality tools > How we think and work

d11:b68.text: The best people hire the best people. Help recruit.

d11:b72.text: The freedom to work remotely allows for more meaningful work.

d0:b150.text: Personal tokens allow you to interact with the API using your own user account. Their permissions mirror what you can do in the monday.com UI, ensuring that API access is consistent with your platform-level permissions.

d0:b155.text: App tokens have an additional set of permission scopes that specify which queries and mutations it can access, while personal tokens have all permission scopes.

d0:b149.text: The monday.com platform API utilizes personal V2 API tokens to authenticate requests and identify the user making the call. These tokens are unique to each user and have no explicit length.

d0:b151.text: If you don't have a monday.com account yet, create a free developer account to get an API token and start testing.

d0:b154.text: For example: If you don't have permission to access a certain workspace via the UI, you won't have permission using your personal API token either.

d0:b170.text: Once you have your token, you can make requests with the API by passing the token in the Authorization header.

d2:b197.text: Fields Type Description Enum Values active_members_count Int The number of active users on the account (includes active users across all products who are not guests or viewers). country_code String The account's two-letter country code in ISO3166 format. The result is based on the location of the account's first admin. created_at Date The account's creation date. first_day_of_the_week FirstDayOfTheWeek! The account's first day of the week. monday sunday id ID! The account's unique identifier. is_during_trial Boolean Whether the account is in a free trial period. is_trial_expired Boolean Whether the account's trial has expired. logo String The account's logo. name String! The account's name. plan Plan The account's payment plan. Returns null for accounts with the multi-product infrastructure. products [AccountProduct] The account's active products. show_timeline_weekends Boolean! Returns true if weekends appear in the timeline. sign_up_product_kind String The product the account first signed up for. slug String! The account's slug. tier String The account's tier.

d7:b183.text: OAuth 2.0 is a protocol that lets your app request authorization to read or modify data in a user's monday account. At the end of the OAuth process, your app gets an access token that belongs to the user and grants access to specified permission scopes.

d7:b192.text: OAuth scopes define what your app can and cannot do. Each endpoint in the monday API requires a certain permission scope, which can be found in our API reference.

d7:b204.text: The first step in the OAuth flow is making an authorization request and redirecting a user to the monday OAuth page. The OAuth request URL is: https://auth.monday.com/oauth2/authorize .

d7:b222.text: Some monday.com users will be part of multiple accounts, so your app may want to specify which account to authorize the user for. In the standard OAuth flow, the user can select the monday.com account where they'd like to authorize using a dropdown menu.

d7:b187.text: monday.com now supports an improved OAuth 2.1 flow with expiring access tokens, refresh tokens, and token revocation. This page describes the current (legacy) flow. If you are building a new integration or want to upgrade your existing app, see Migrating to the new OAuth 2.1 flow .

d7:b202.text: Your app's backend sends a POST to the token request endpoint with this code. The token endpoint will respond with an access token. The access token gives your app access to the monday API on behalf of the user and will be valid until the user uninstalls your app.

d7:b211.text: Once you have obtained an authorization code from the authorization endpoint, you can exchange it for an access token to make calls to monday’s API. The authorization code is only valid for 10 minutes, after which you will have to make another request to get another code.

d9:b184.text: Building an app for monday.com? This guide walks you through the complete development process, from initial concept to marketplace launch. Whether you're creating your first integration or expanding your existing app's capabilities, follow this structured approach to ensure success.

d9:b185.text: Your monday app development journey consists of four distinct phases, each with specific goals:

d9:b199.text: Goal: Define what you're building and why it matters to users

d9:b200.text: In this phase, you'll identify the specific problem your app solves and how it creates value for monday.com users. The most successful apps integrate seamlessly into existing workflows and are part of a broader solution, rather than standalone tools.

d9:b214.text: At monday.com, our goal is to foster a robust, innovative, and high-quality ecosystem that delivers maximum value to our users. To ensure the marketplace remains a curated space of distinct, impactful solutions, we are updating our submission review criteria.

d9:b215.text: Moving forward, the app review team will no longer accept submissions that duplicate existing ecosystem functionality or integrations.

d9:b216.text: New Rejection Criteria: To maintain our high standards, apps falling into the following categories will be rejected during the review process:

d9:b217.text: Redundant Third-Party Integrations We will no longer approve apps whose primary purpose is to integrate monday.com with a third-party product that already has an active integration in the marketplace. This includes, but is not limited to, new apps targeting:

d9:b226.text: Any other existing integration currently available in the marketplace

d9:b227.text: Functional Duplication ("Clone" Apps) We will no longer accept apps that copy the core functionality of an existing marketplace app.

d9:b228.text: Note on Value Add: Making slight UI tweaks, minor feature additions, or superficial changes to an existing app's concept will not be considered "new value." Your app must introduce a substantially unique solution or serve an entirely different workflow to be approved.

d9:b230.text: Before you begin developing a new app, we strongly recommend that you thoroughly search the monday.com marketplace to ensure your concept does not conflict with these new guidelines.

d9:b241.text: Not sure what to build? Check out our idea board for community-requested features and emerging opportunities.

d9:b256.text: New apps built primarily using no-code platforms or AI-generated “vibe code” are not eligible for marketplace approval.

Over time, top-rated apps will be considered when awarding labels and badges, influencing search results, creating premium marketplace categories, and appearing in app recommendations.

d10:b184.text: To increase your score, focus on delivering a great user experience and building strong relationships with your customers.

d10:b186.text: When discussing ratings and reviews, it's important to understand the difference between the terms:

d10:b187.text: Rating: A numeric value between 1 and 5 stars; submitted by a single app user

d10:b188.text: Review: An optional written opinion, submitted alongside a rating

d10:b189.text: App rating: The average of all submitted ratings

d10:b191.text: Users can submit ratings between 1 and 5 stars, where 1 is the lowest and 5 is the highest. They can also leave an optional text review. Individual ratings and reviews are publicly visible in the app marketplace.

d10:b195.text: Once your app has received at least five ratings, they are combined to form an app rating (the average score displayed on your app listing page). This minimum threshold helps prevent disproportionate impact from a small number of submissions and ensures the rating reflects overall user sentiment.

d10:b198.text: Ratings can be updated at any time, and any updates will overwrite the previous submission.

d10:b201.text: You can access review information in the Reviews tab. There, you will see your app rating, along with a breakdown of individual ratings and reviews.

d10:b203.text: Customers can see an app's ratings and reviews on your app's marketplace listing page. They can also see your average app rating across all apps on the Partner Page .

d10:b205.text: Ratings are integral to your app’s success, but they only matter if users leave them. We've developed several methods to encourage users to leave ratings.

d10:b206.text: Send the user a custom URL

d10:b207.text: One of the best ways to prompt users to rate your app is through a custom URL . The URL will direct users directly to your app with the rating pop-up open, allowing them to quickly and easily leave a rating and review.

d10:b210.text: Prompt the user in your app

d10:b214.text: In addition to developer-initiated prompts, monday.com also automatically collects ratings by prompting users when they open the Installed Apps page. The pop-up only appears once, even if users close out of it without rating the app. You do not need to implement anything in your app for this method.

d11:b183.text: Users create a subscription when they sign up for a trial, free, or paid plan with your app (depending on your app's plan tiers). Each subscription serves as a billing contract between the user and your app. Every monday.com account can only have one active subscription per app.

d11:b229.text: The finance team reviews your invoice within 7 business days. After approval, the status changes to “Approved by revenue.” No further action is required from you after this step.

d11:b233.text: Once the payment is processed, the status updates to “Paid.” Funds typically arrive in your Payoneer account within a few business days.

d11:b237.text: If there's an issue with your invoice, the finance team will update the status to “Need another check” and leave a comment describing the problem. Once resolved, the review process restarts from the “Invoice uploaded” step.

d11:b257.text: All app subscriptions automatically renew . If a payment method fails on the renewal date, the account enters a 45-day grace period to update the payment information. The app will continue to function during the 45-day period.

d11:b260.text: Uninstalling an app does not automatically cancel the app subscription. Accounts can reinstall the app before the renewal date to regain access. If reinstalled after the renewal date, the user must purchase a new subscription.

d11:b264.text: If a user cancels their monday.com plan, their app subscriptions will automatically be cancelled.

d11:b195.text: You can also track your app's subscriptions using your shared payment board. After monetization is implemented and your app receives marketplace approval, monday.com will invite you to this board.
